skills.name: Imputation fitted before the split
skills.question: Does filling missing values on the whole dataset before splitting flatter the result?
skills.metric_meaning: What a practitioner would report after cross-validation.

careless.label: medians and modes from every row

skills.verdict: no difference this experiment can resolve
skills.explanation: A median computed over all rows carries a little information from the rows that will become the validation fold. A fifth of ages are missing here, so there is something to carry -- but a median is a robust statistic, and leaving out a fifth of the rows rarely moves it, which bounds how much can leak.
pitfalls: Calling fillna on the full frame before any split.
Imputing with a statistic computed outside the pipeline, then cross-validating the pipeline.

skills.name: Scaling fitted before the split
skills.question: Does standardising on the whole dataset before splitting flatter the result?
skills.metric_meaning: What a practitioner would report after cross-validation.

careless.label: mean and standard deviation from every row

skills.verdict: no difference this experiment can resolve
skills.explanation: The scaler sees the validation rows' mean and spread. For a linear model scored by a ranking metric, standardising is an affine change of the inputs that the fit undoes, so the two versions agree to floating-point precision. The leak is real and its effect here is nil.
pitfalls: Scaling once at the top of a notebook and splitting afterwards.

skills.name: Feature selection before the split
skills.question: Does choosing features using every row flatter the result?
skills.metric_meaning: What a practitioner would report after cross-validation.

careless.label: eight features chosen using every row

skills.verdict: the careless version flatters the result
skills.explanation: Selection is a model decision. Ranking features by how well they separate the target on all rows lets the validation folds influence which features exist at all.
pitfalls: Running SelectKBest once, then cross-validating the reduced matrix.
Dropping low-correlation features after looking at the whole dataset.

skills.name: Target encoding without out-of-fold means
skills.question: How much does a target encoder flatter the result if a row's own label is in its encoding?
skills.metric_meaning: What a practitioner would report after cross-validation.

careless.label: category means from the full training set

careful.label: each row encoded from the other folds

skills.verdict: the careless version flatters the result
skills.explanation: A category mean that includes the row being encoded carries that row's label. Rare categories are the worst case: a category appearing once is encoded as its own answer.
pitfalls: Encoding before splitting, which is the usual way this is written.
Forgetting that a category seen once becomes a perfect predictor of its own row.

skills.name: Oversampling before the split
skills.question: What happens when duplicated minority rows end up in both training and validation?
skills.metric_meaning: What a practitioner would report after cross-validation.
skills.verdict: the careless version flatters the result
skills.explanation: Random oversampling copies minority rows. Copies made before splitting land on both sides, so the model is scored partly on rows it memorised.
pitfalls: Balancing the dataset as a preparation step, before any split.
The same applies to SMOTE, whose synthetic rows interpolate between neighbours that may be split apart.

skills.name: The same oversampling, with a linear model
skills.question: Does the cost of duplicated rows depend on the model they are given to?
skills.metric_meaning: What a practitioner would report after cross-validation.
skills.verdict: no difference this experiment can resolve
skills.explanation: The mistake is identical to the entry above; only the model changes. A logistic regression has nowhere to store an individual row, so a duplicate on both sides of the split cannot be recognised. Read the two entries together: how much a leak costs is a property of the pipeline, not of the mistake alone.
pitfalls: Assuming a leak is harmless because it was harmless with a linear model.
Assuming a leak is fatal because it was fatal with a nearest-neighbour or tree model.

skills.name: Choosing the decision threshold on the test set
skills.question: How much does picking the best threshold on the test set overstate the score?
skills.metric_meaning: The F1 a practitioner would publish.

careless.label: threshold that maximises F1 on the held-out set

careful.label: threshold chosen on a validation split

skills.verdict: the careless version flatters the result
skills.explanation: The threshold is a parameter like any other. Choosing it against the test set tunes the model to that particular sample.
pitfalls: Sweeping thresholds against the test labels and reporting the maximum.
Reporting the best point on a precision-recall curve drawn from the test set.

skills.name: Reporting the best of several models on the test set
skills.question: How much does trying twelve models and reporting the best test score overstate it?
skills.metric: ROC AUC on the held-out set
skills.metric_meaning: The AUC a practitioner would publish.

careless.label: best of twelve on the held-out set

careful.label: chosen on validation, then scored once

skills.verdict: the careless version flatters the result
skills.explanation: Each model's test score carries noise. Taking the maximum of twelve selects partly for the model and partly for the luckiest noise.
pitfalls: Comparing models on the test set and reporting the winner's score.
Repeating an experiment until it gives a good number.

skills.name: Splitting rows that belong to the same group
skills.question: Do family members on both sides of a split flatter the result?
skills.metric: ROC AUC on the held-out set
skills.metric_meaning: The AUC a practitioner would publish.
skills.verdict: no difference this experiment can resolve
skills.explanation: Passengers travelling together share a ticket, a cabin and often a fate. A random split puts relatives on both sides, so the model can recognise a family rather than learn who survived.
pitfalls: Splitting rows when the unit that repeats is a person, household or session.
Assuming rows are independent because each is one line in a file.

skills.name: Trusting one train/test split
skills.question: How far does a single split's score wander from a cross-validated one?
skills.metric_meaning: One split's score against the mean of five folds, on the same data.
skills.verdict: no difference this experiment can resolve
skills.explanation: Neither is careless; the point is the spread. On a few hundred rows one split's score moves by several points from seed to seed, which is wider than most differences people report between models.
pitfalls: Comparing two models on a single split of a small dataset.
Reporting a score without saying how it would move under another split.

skills.name: Reading accuracy on an imbalanced target
skills.question: What does accuracy hide when one class is rare?
skills.metric_meaning: Two readings of the same predictions.
skills.verdict: the careless version flatters the result
skills.explanation: Fewer than a quarter of donors gave again, so predicting 'no' for everyone is right most of the time. Balanced accuracy averages the two classes' recall and gives that strategy 0.5.
pitfalls: Reporting accuracy on a target where one class is rare.
Choosing a model by accuracy when the rare class is the one that matters.

skills.name: Calibrating predicted probabilities
skills.question: Does isotonic calibration improve the probabilities, or only the story?
skills.metric_meaning: Mean squared error of the predicted probabilities.
skills.verdict: the careless version really is worse
skills.explanation: Ranking and probability are different goals. A model can order applicants well and still give probabilities that are systematically too confident. Calibration is fitted on training data only.
pitfalls: Reading a predicted probability as a frequency without checking calibration.
Calibrating on the test set, which is the same mistake as tuning a threshold there.
